lines.text: Giant stone heads, pyramids and a city on a lake, then conquest, independence and revolution. This is the story of Mexico.
More than three thousand years ago, on the Gulf coast, the Olmecs carved colossal stone heads, a mother culture for all that came after.
Near today's capital rose Teotihuacan, a vast planned city with the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon. Its builders remain unknown by name.
In the southern rainforest, the Maya city of Palenque raised temples and the tomb of its ruler Pakal, its carved texts full of history.
In the Yucatan, Chichen Itza grew around its stepped pyramid and great ball court, a centre of trade and ritual.
After Teotihuacan fell, the Toltecs flourished at Tula. Later Aztecs remembered them as master builders and artists.
In 1325 the Mexica founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco, joined to the shore by long causeways.
At its heart stood the Templo Mayor, with twin shrines to the gods of war and rain.
Allied with two other cities, Tenochtitlan built the Aztec Empire, gathering tribute from many peoples, with great markets and schools.
Old ways of honouring the dead would blend with Catholic feast days into the Day of the Dead, with its altars, flowers and food.
In 1519 Hernan Cortes landed. With many Indigenous allies, and helped by disease, the Spanish took Tenochtitlan two years later.
On the ruins rose Mexico City, capital of New Spain, a viceroyalty that reached from Central America to the Philippines.
In 1531, tradition says, the Virgin appeared to Juan Diego. Our Lady of Guadalupe became Mexico's best-loved symbol of faith.
In the seventeenth century the nun Sor Juana, largely self-taught, wrote poems, plays and a famous defence of women's right to study.
The priest Miguel Hidalgo would one September morning call his parishioners to rise against Spain.
Benito Juarez, a lawyer of Zapotec origin, would become president, limit the church's power and lead the fight against a foreign emperor.
Hidalgo's cry came in 1810. He was executed a year later, but the fight went on for eleven years.
In 1821 Mexico was free. Today it is the largest Spanish-speaking country on Earth.
Porfirio Diaz, a general, would rule for over thirty years, building railways while the poor lost their land.
After the United States annexed Texas, war followed. Mexico lost about half its territory, including California.
Then France invaded and crowned Maximilian of Austria emperor. Juarez resisted, and in 1867 Maximilian was defeated and shot.
Pancho Villa would lead the Division of the North in the revolution, and even raid a town across the border.
In Morelos, the farmer Emiliano Zapata would fight to give village lands back to the people who worked them.
Diego Rivera would cover public walls with scenes of Mexican history and its workers.
And Frida Kahlo, injured in a bus accident as a girl, would paint self-portraits of pain, identity and Mexican life.
In 1910 the revolution broke out and Diaz fell. A decade of fighting over land and power led to the constitution of 1917.
The poet Octavio Paz would explore Mexican identity in The Labyrinth of Solitude and win the Nobel Prize.
After the revolution, the government gave artists the walls of public buildings, and Mexican muralism was born.
In 1929 a new party united the revolution's factions. It would hold the presidency without a break for over seventy years.
In 1938 President Lazaro Cardenas took over the foreign oil firms, and the state company Pemex was formed.
A year later Kahlo painted The Two Fridas, two versions of herself side by side, their hearts joined by a vein.
In 1962 Claudia Sheinbaum was born. A scientist and later mayor of Mexico City, she would make history.
In 1968 Mexico City hosted the Olympics, where records fell in the thin air and two sprinters raised their fists against racism.
Two years later, Pele's Brazil won the World Cup in Mexico, the first shown in colour on television.
In September 1985 a great earthquake struck. The old lakebed amplified the shaking, buildings fell and thousands died.
Months later Mexico hosted the World Cup again, and Maradona's two famous goals against England carried Argentina to the title.
In 1994 Mexico opened its trade with the north, joining the United States and Canada in a free trade pact.
In 2006 the state declared war on the drug cartels, a fight that has cost hundreds of thousands of lives.
In 2024 Mexicans elected Claudia Sheinbaum, the first woman president in the country's history.
And in 2026 Mexico shared the first World Cup held across three countries, which Spain went on to win.
From Olmec stone to a woman president, Mexico carries its long past into every new chapter.
